full_citation: Castleman, J., Shen, Z., Metevier, B., Springer, M., & Korolova, A. (2026). Measuring validity in LLM-based resume screening. arXiv:2602.18550.
population_categories: Demographic groups (not detailed in abstract)
manipulation: Constructed comparable resumes with known ground-truth superiority
outcome: Ranking validity; abstention; group selection rates
main_result: Many models fail to consistently pick the more qualified resume; do not reliably abstain when candidates are equally qualified; select groups at different rates, sometimes favouring marginalised groups
limitations: Preprint
relation_to_project: Supports a manipulation check that models distinguish our qualification tiers (positive control) and pre-registering tie/abstention handling in forced choice

full_citation: Gao, Z., Jiang, W., & Yan, Y. (2026). Can LLMs hire fairly? Racial bias in resume screening. arXiv:2606.28978.
population_categories: US; race, gender
manipulation: Paired-resume method of Kline, Rose & Walters (2022)
main_result: The one 2023-vintage model reproduces a pro-White gap (+2.12 pp); every 2024+ model shows a null gap or a significant pro-Black reversal (up to -3.01 pp); same pattern for gender
limitations: Preprint; US race/gender
relation_to_project: Expect possible reversals and vintage effects: two-sided hypotheses, record exact model ids and dates

full_citation: Hoffmann, M., Jouffroy, E., Jouanneau, W., Palyart, M., & Pebereau, C. (2026). Evaluating LLM Behavior in Hiring: Implicit Weights, Fairness Across Groups, and Alignment with Human Preferences. arXiv:2601.11379.
models_or_system: Gemini 2.0 Flash; prompts in French; 3 scorings per pair averaged
population_categories: First names signalling European male, European female and Arabic male (one pooled 'Arabic-sounding' group; Arabic female names excluded for low prevalence); bachelor vs master
manipulation: Full factorial synthetic freelancer profiles built from a major European online freelance marketplace, crossed with project briefs; productivity signals (skills, experience, reputation, rate, work arrangement) and demographic markers varied independently
outcome: Hiring probability on a 10-point scale; OLS implicit weights with interactions
main_result: Productivity signals dominate; Arabic-sounding (and female) names have small, non-significant average effects (+0.001 and +0.002 points); interactions show a small baseline penalty for Arabic male profiles when all characteristics match (-0.026 points), more tolerance for experience gaps, and stronger penalties for weak platform reputation; female and Arabic profiles rated slightly lower for remote contracts
limitations: Preprint; one model; names, not nationality; one pooled Arabic group; freelance marketplace rather than employee hiring
relation_to_project: Second LLM hiring study with a pooled 'Arab' name group (after lippens2024computer): again no disaggregation by Arab origin; near-zero average effects can hide interactions with qualification signals, supporting our tier x nationality checks
novelty_threat_reason: Pooled Arabic-name group in a freelance-fit task; no national-origin manipulation and no within-Arab estimand

full_citation: Leininger, C., Veit, H., Assenmacher, M., & Bender, A. (2026). Fairness beyond anonymization? Demographic leakage in German LLM-generated resumes. arXiv:2609.22188 (BIAS 2026 workshop at ECML PKDD).
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv comment: accepted at BIAS 2026 workshop @ ECML PKDD)
population_categories: Germany; gender- and ethnicity-associated names (German vs Turkish, per paper HTML snippet)
manipulation: Names varied when an LLM generates German resumes from anonymised job-matching profiles; then anonymisation and downstream leakage classifiers
outcome: Recoverability of gender/ethnicity from generated, anonymised resumes
main_result: Gender reliably recoverable even after anonymisation (subtle German word choice); ethnicity leakage comparatively weak
limitations: Generation/leakage, not screening decisions; no Arab origins
relation_to_project: German-language LLM hiring context (Qwen3) using Turkish as the migrant-origin category (supports the Turkish benchmark); our CVs are rendered deterministically from fixed templates, so generation leakage does not apply
novelty_threat_reason: Leakage in resume generation, not screening decisions by nationality; no Arab origins

full_citation: Leyva-Vazquez, M., & Smarandache, F. (2026). Institutional Prestige as Geographic Bias in Large Language Models: Evidence from Three Factorial Experiments with Bootstrap Confidence Intervals. arXiv:2608.18107.
venue: arXiv preprint (extended version of a Spanish-language paper in Neutrosophic Computing and Machine Learning, per arXiv comment)
population_categories: Applicant name ethnicity; institution prestige tier; country of origin (two levels in Study 2; the abstract's examples are MIT and the University of Guayaquil)
manipulation: Three factorial candidate-evaluation experiments across five professional domains: 3x4 name origin x institution tier; 2x2 prestige x country; 2x2 journal x institution
main_result: Institution-tier gradient +0.297 points (95% bootstrap CI 0.175 to 0.422) while name-origin effects are negligible; prestige effect (+0.185) exceeds the country-of-origin effect (+0.126, CI 0.037 to 0.218); journal prestige dominates institutional prestige
limitations: Preprint; academic-style candidate profiles; country factor has two levels; no Arab origins
relation_to_project: 2026 candidate-evaluation audit in which a country-of-origin signal shifts LLM scores even where names do not; supports holding education institutions constant (German) across clones; another case where national origin appears with only a handful of levels
novelty_threat_reason: Country of origin varied at two levels, no Arab countries, no within-region estimand

full_citation: Pavlopoulos, V. (2026). Minimal but conditional: Auditing demographic bias in large language model resume evaluation across commercial and open-weight models. Analytics, 5(3), 30.
population_categories: Gender, race (plus age-related artefact)
manipulation: Reference-anchored comparison against a fixed neutral reference resume; provocation conditions (weaker candidates, relaxed prompt, culture-fit language)
main_result: Gender and race effects negligible under all conditions (equivalence tests vs a justified smallest effect of interest; FDR control; mixed-effects models for clustered repeated evaluations); a seniority positive control confirmed sensitivity; the open-weight model reacted to a few explicit minority-status signals
limitations: Three models; MDPI journal
relation_to_project: Design template: positive control (our qualification tiers), equivalence testing so nulls are informative, mixed models for repeated evaluations; explicit signals matter for open-weight models (our main compute)

full_citation: Rozado, D. (2026). Gender and positional biases in LLM-based hiring decisions: Evidence from comparative CV/resume evaluations. PeerJ Computer Science, 12, e3628.
population_categories: Gender (male/female first names; explicit gender field; pronouns)
manipulation: Pairs of profession-matched CVs, each pair shown twice with names swapped; variants with explicit gender field, neutral labels (Candidate A/B), pronouns; isolated rating
sample_size: 30,800 decisions (22 models x 70 professions x 10 job descriptions x 2 orders); 30,690 analysed
main_result: Female-named candidates chosen 56.9% vs 43.1%; adding an explicit gender field increased the female preference; first-listed candidate chosen 63.5% vs 36.5% (21 of 22 models individually significant); isolated ratings showed a negligible gender effect; random temperature U(0,1) per pair, same for both orders
limitations: Gender only; synthetic CVs generated by LLMs
relation_to_project: Strongest support for our quad design (swap attributes and both orders); explicit attribute fields amplify effects (our Nationality line is explicit); pairwise and isolated designs can disagree, so both arms are needed

full_citation: Tan, B. C. Z., Khoo, S., Doan, B. N., Liu, Z., Chen, N. F., & Lee, R. K.-W. (2026). Small changes, big impact: Demographic bias in LLM-based hiring through subtle sociocultural markers in anonymised resumes. arXiv:2603.05189 (arXiv comment: EMNLP 2026).
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv comment states EMNLP 2026; proceedings not yet checked)
population_categories: Singapore; 4 ethnicities x 2 genders signalled by job-irrelevant markers
manipulation: Job-irrelevant sociocultural markers (languages, co-curricular activities, volunteering, hobbies) on anonymised resumes; 1v1 comparison and score-and-shortlist; with/without rationale prompting
outcome: Pairwise choices; top-score / shortlist rates; demographic inference F1
main_result: Models recover demographics from markers with high F1; favour markers associated with Chinese and Caucasian males; language markers alone suffice to infer ethnicity; asking for explanations may amplify bias
limitations: Singapore context; indirect signals; no nationality field
relation_to_project: Justifies holding languages constant across clones (German C2, English C1, no Arabic); both pairwise and score formats are needed; our required 'reason' field could itself shift decisions (explore by condition)
novelty_threat_reason: Ethnicity via sociocultural proxies in Singapore; no national-origin or Arab categories

full_citation: An, J., Huang, D., Lin, C., & Tai, M. (2025). Measuring gender and racial biases in large language models: Intersectional evidence from automated resume evaluation. PNAS Nexus, 4(3), pgaf089.
models_or_system: GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3-70b
population_categories: US; gender x race (Black/White and others) via randomized social identities
manipulation: Randomized applicant identities on otherwise comparable entry-level resumes
outcome: Assessment score; implied hiring probability at a threshold
main_result: Higher scores for female candidates; lower scores for Black male candidates; ~1-3 pp differences in hiring probability at a threshold; direction/magnitude vary by model
limitations: US race/gender only; name-based identity; no nationality or religion
relation_to_project: Template for large-scale independent scoring and for translating score gaps into threshold-based interview gaps; supports reporting both score and interview decision
novelty_threat_reason: Different construct (US race/gender), no national-origin or Arab categories

full_citation: Bilon, X. J. (2025). Sociodemographic biases in employment decision-making by large language models: experimental evidence from ChatGPT simulations. Journal of Decision Systems, 34(1), 2599912.
models_or_system: ChatGPT; three model versions x three temperature settings
population_categories: Age, gender, sexuality, national origin (country levels not stated in the abstract; abstract contrasts U.S. vs non-U.S. applicants)
manipulation: Full factorial design on standardised resumes across two job types; hiring-likelihood scores elicited with structured prompts
main_result: Significant but variable differences on all four dimensions; women and gay or lesbian candidates received higher scores in some settings but not others; older and non-U.S. applicants almost consistently received lower scores
limitations: Full text not accessible (publisher 403), so national-origin levels remain unverified; one model family
relation_to_project: Another hiring audit with a national-origin factor; supports the claim that when origin appears in LLM hiring audits it is coarse (U.S. vs non-U.S. per abstract); read the full text before citing any country-level detail
novelty_threat_reason: Abstract reports only a U.S. vs non-U.S. contrast; would become a threat only if the full text disaggregates several Arab countries (unverified)

full_citation: Busetta, G., Campolo, M. G., & Ficarra, G. M. (2025). Artificial Intelligence and Discrimination: A Vignette Experiment of Labour Market Discrimination in Large Language Models. In Statistics for Innovation II (Italian Statistical Society Series on Advances in Statistics), 303-308. Springer.
venue: Statistics for Innovation II (Springer proceedings chapter)
models_or_system: Le Chat, ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, MetaAI
population_categories: Sex, ethnicity (levels not stated in abstract), education, age
manipulation: Factorial survey (vignette) experiment on candidate profiles
main_result: None of the six models shows gender bias; ChatGPT, Grok and DeepSeek show signs of ethnic discrimination to varying degrees; framed as taste-based vs statistical discrimination
limitations: Six-page proceedings chapter; ethnicity levels and country context not stated in the abstract
relation_to_project: Multi-model vignette hiring audit with an ethnicity factor; supports expecting model-specific effects; per abstract it does not vary nationality or individual Arab origins
novelty_threat_reason: Ethnicity factor with unknown levels and no nationality manipulation per abstract; would matter only if its ethnic levels were several Arab origins (unverified)

full_citation: Geiger, R. S., O'Sullivan, F., Wang, E., & Lo, J. (2025). Asking an AI for salary negotiation advice is a matter of concern: Controlled experimental perturbation of ChatGPT for protected and non-protected group discrimination on a contextual task with no clear ground truth answers. PLOS ONE, 20(2), e0318500.
population_categories: Gender (pronouns), 50 US universities (incl. fictional), 19 majors; employee vs employer voice
manipulation: Controlled perturbation of salary-negotiation prompts
main_result: Significant gender gaps (smaller than for other attributes); largest gaps between model versions and between employee- vs employer-voiced prompts; university/major effects inconsistent across versions
limitations: US-only; no nationality manipulation
relation_to_project: SEED CORRECTION: this study does NOT vary nationality (US universities only, per the paper). Useful only for model-version instability and prompt-voice sensitivity

full_citation: Iso, H., Pezeshkpour, P., Bhutani, N., & Hruschka, E. (2025). Evaluating bias in LLMs for job-resume matching: Gender, race, and education. In Proceedings of NAACL 2025 (Volume 3: Industry Track), 672-683.
population_categories: US/English; gender, race, educational background
manipulation: Attribute perturbations in job-resume matching
main_result: Recent models reduced bias on explicit gender/race attributes; implicit bias related to educational background remains significant
limitations: English/US only
relation_to_project: Recent models may show small explicit-attribute effects; supports equivalence-style reporting and holding education constant (German institutions across clones)

full_citation: Phutane, M., Jung, H., Kim, M. J., et al. (2025). ABLEIST: Intersectional Disability Bias in LLM-Generated Hiring Scenarios. arXiv:2510.10998.
models_or_system: Six LLMs (incl. Claude-3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-chat)
population_categories: Disability x gender x nationality (American, Indian) x caste (Brahmin, Dalit)
manipulation: Generated hiring conversations for varied candidate profiles
main_result: Substantial increases in ableist and intersectional harms toward disabled candidates, often not detected by existing tools
limitations: Nationality has only two levels (US, India)
relation_to_project: Shows 'nationality' in hiring audits often means a US/India contrast, not many origins

full_citation: Rao, P. S. B., Venkatesan, L. N., Cherubini, M., & Jayagopi, D. B. (2025). Invisible Filters: Cultural Bias in Hiring Evaluations Using Large Language Models. Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, 8(3), 2164-2176.
population_categories: UK vs Indian job seekers; names varied by gender, caste, region within Indian set
manipulation: Scoring of real interview transcripts; controlled name substitutions
main_result: Indian transcripts scored consistently lower even when anonymised, linked to linguistic features; name substitutions alone had no significant effect
limitations: Cross-national difference arises from transcript language, not a nationality signal
relation_to_project: Caution: name-only manipulations can show nulls; our explicit nationality field is a stronger, more transparent cue
novelty_threat_reason: UK vs India; no Arab origins

full_citation: Sorokovikova, A., Chizhov, P., Eremenko, I., & Yamshchikov, I. P. (2025). Surface Fairness, Deep Bias: A Comparative Study of Bias in Language Models. In Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Gender Bias in NLP (GeBNLP), pp. 206-227.
models_or_system: Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o Mini, Qwen 2.5 Plus, Mixtral 8x22B, Llama 3.1 8B
population_categories: Persona sex; ethnicity (Asian, Black, Hispanic, White); migrant type (expatriate, migrant, refugee)
manipulation: Pre-prompted personae on MMLU; grading user answers; salary negotiation advice
main_result: Negligible MMLU differences; grading shows more bias; salary advice shows pronounced bias (e.g., expatriates higher, refugees lower)
limitations: No nationality/country manipulation
relation_to_project: SEED CORRECTION: does NOT vary nationality. Relevant only because migration-status framing (refugee) may be part of what some Arab nationality signals evoke (e.g., Syrian, Yemeni, Sudanese)

full_citation: Wen, A., Patil, T., Saxena, A., Fu, Y., O'Brien, S., & Zhu, K. (2025). FAIRE: Assessing racial and gender bias in AI-driven resume evaluations. arXiv:2504.01420.
population_categories: Race, gender
manipulation: Resumes slightly altered to reflect racial or gender identities
main_result: Every model shows some bias; magnitude and direction vary considerably
limitations: Preprint; no national origin
relation_to_project: Supports measuring both independent scoring and comparative ranking (our baseline + forced choice)

full_citation: An, H., Acquaye, C., Wang, C., Li, Z., & Rudinger, R. (2024). Do large language models discriminate in hiring decisions on the basis of race, ethnicity, and gender? In Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 2: Short Papers), 386-397.
population_categories: US; race/ethnicity (White, Hispanic, others) x gender via first names
manipulation: Applicant first name in templated prompts asking the LLM to write an acceptance or rejection email
outcome: Probability of generating an acceptance vs rejection email
main_result: Many settings favour White over Hispanic applicants; masculine White names highest and masculine Hispanic names lowest acceptance; comparative rates vary across templates (idiosyncratic, prompt-sensitive)
limitations: Name-only signal; no CV content; US groups only
relation_to_project: Warns that group rankings are prompt-sensitive: supports fixed, versioned templates and robustness across prompt conditions

full_citation: Armstrong, L., Liu, A., MacNeil, S., & Metaxa, D. (2024). The Silicon Ceiling: Auditing GPT's race and gender biases in hiring. In Proceedings of the 4th ACM Conference on Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization (EAAMO '24), 1-18.
population_categories: US; 4 racial groups x 2 genders via 32 names; plus 2 'anonymous' controls
manipulation: Name at top of resume (Study 1 assessment); name-conditioned resume generation (Study 2)
sample_size: Study 1: 320 resumes x 3 prompts x 50 trials = 48,000 scores; Study 2: 320 generated resumes
outcome: Overall rating, willingness to interview, hireability scores; coded content of generated resumes
main_result: Some stereotype-consistent biases in scoring; generated resumes for Asian and Hispanic names carried immigrant markers (non-native English, non-US education/work)
limitations: Single model; 'anonymous' controls behaved inconsistently and were dropped from analysis
relation_to_project: (1) Used 50 repeated trials analysed with name as a random effect: precedent for treating repetitions as within-stimulus; (2) anonymous controls were unstable: warns our not_stated control is not a neutral baseline; (3) models link origin to non-native language: supports holding languages constant

full_citation: Gaebler, J. D., Goel, S., Huq, A. Z., & Tambe, P. B. (2024). Auditing large language models for race & gender disparities: Implications for artificial intelligence-based hiring. Behavioral Science & Policy, 10(2), 46-55.
venue: Behavioral Science & Policy (print Oct 2024; online Mar 2025)
url_doi_arxiv: https://doi.org/10.1177/23794607251320229 (preprint arXiv:2404.03086, 'Auditing the Use of Language Models to Guide Hiring Decisions')
models_or_system: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8x7B, Claude Instant, Claude 2, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet (arXiv version)
population_categories: US; race (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian) x gender via names and pronouns
manipulation: Real K-12 teaching applications edited to signal demographics via names/pronouns (correspondence design)
main_result: Moderate disparities, models slightly favouring women and non-White candidates; robust to prompt variants incl. an added EEOC anti-discrimination statement (robustness run on GPT-3.5); blinding names had little effect; LLMs infer demographics from blinded materials
limitations: Single application domain; robustness checks on one model; correspondence method audits only the manipulated channel
relation_to_project: Anti-discrimination instruction did not remove disparities: sets expectation for our neutrality condition; direction can reverse relative to human audits (post-training): pre-register two-sided tests
novelty_threat_reason: Race/gender in US teaching hires; no national origin

full_citation: Lippens, L. (2024). Computer says 'no': Exploring systemic bias in ChatGPT using an audit approach. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, 2(1), 100054.
venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
models_or_system: GPT-3.5 (13 June 2023 snapshot) via API; prompts in Dutch
population_categories: Flanders/Belgium; 9 name-signalled groups: Arab, Asian, Black American, Central African, Dutch (reference), Eastern European, Hispanic, Turkish, White American; x gender
manipulation: Correspondence-audit CV screening: validated ethnic names on otherwise identical CVs matched to real VDAB vacancies; nationality field held constant ('Belgian'); isolated prompts (no side-by-side comparison)
main_result: All minority groups scored below Dutch-named candidates (about -0.96 to -2.42 points on 1-100); Arab -1.41 (SE 0.21), Turkish -1.75; largest penalty for Eastern Europeans; discrimination ratios at a cutoff of 75: 0.85 Arabs, 0.86 Turks. The author's comparison with human audits: smaller penalties than worldwide human averages for Arabs (0.59) and Turks (0.75) and than Belgian human audits for Arabs (0.79), but about equal to Belgian audits for Turks (0.85), and larger than human benchmarks for Hispanics (worldwide 0.92) and Black candidates (Belgium 1.00). Ethnic discrimination more pronounced than gender discrimination and mainly in jobs with favourable labour conditions or higher language-proficiency requirements; temperature varied between 0 and 1.5 in about two-fifths of prompts
limitations: Single model; 'Arab' pooled as one name group drawn from several name sources; names bundle ethnicity, religion, gender and name-frequency effects; nationality fixed as Belgian; Dutch/Flemish framing; OLS on scores
relation_to_project: Closest LLM hiring audit and the most important precedent: same correspondence paradigm in a European setting with Arab and Turkish groups, but treats Arab as ONE category - exactly the pooling our design tests; we differ by an explicit nationality line (not names), 22 individual origins, a German context, several open-weight models and a within-Arab estimand
novelty_threat_reason: Already shows Arab and Turkish penalties in an LLM European CV audit, so 'LLMs penalise Arab applicants' is not new; our novelty rests on disaggregating Arab into 22 national-origin signals via an explicit nationality field

full_citation: Nakano, T., Shimari, K., Kula, R. G., Treude, C., Cheong, M., & Matsumoto, K. (2024). Nigerian Software Engineer or American Data Scientist? GitHub Profile Recruitment Bias in Large Language Models. In 2024 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME), 624-629.
population_categories: Developer location: United States, India, Nigeria, Poland
manipulation: Select a six-person team from real GitHub profiles (login, bio, location) from four countries; counterfactual swaps of the location string between profiles
sample_size: 3,657 profiles (2019-2023); 100 selection runs; about 2,300 counterfactual runs
outcome: Selection frequency by region; assigned developer role
main_result: Preference for some regions over others (significant US vs Nigeria and US vs Poland differences), persisting when location strings are swapped; roles assigned by country (e.g. US profiles as data scientists, many Nigerian profiles as junior developers)
limitations: Early-results paper; real profiles (content fixed only within the swap); four countries, none Arab; one model
relation_to_project: Closest precedent for swapping only a country string on an otherwise fixed profile in LLM recruitment: supports the one-line counterfactual design; no Arab origins
novelty_threat_reason: Country-of-origin string swap in LLM recruitment, but four non-Arab countries and no within-region estimand

full_citation: Nghiem, H., Prindle, J., Zhao, J., & Daume III, H. (2024). "You gotta be a doctor, Lin": An investigation of name-based bias of large language models in employment recommendations. In Proceedings of EMNLP 2024, 7268-7287.
population_categories: US; race x gender via 320 first names
manipulation: First name in hiring and salary prompts across 40 occupations
main_result: Preference for White female-sounding names; salary recommendations vary by up to 5% between subgroups with identical qualifications
limitations: Names only; US categories
relation_to_project: Large per-group sampling as precedent; salary gap as secondary outcome type (not used by us)

full_citation: Wang, Z., Wu, Z., Guan, X., Thaler, M., Koshiyama, A., Lu, S., Beepath, S., Ertekin, E., & Perez-Ortiz, M. (2024). JobFair: A framework for benchmarking gender hiring bias in large language models. In Findings of EMNLP 2024, 3227-3246.
population_categories: Gender
manipulation: Gender counterfactuals on resumes across industries
outcome: Resume scores; Rank After Scoring; impact ratio
main_result: Level bias vs spread (variance) bias; taste-based vs statistical decomposition; 7 of 10 LLMs biased against males in at least one industry; bias invariant to resume content for 8 of 10
limitations: Gender only
relation_to_project: Supports analysing variance (spread) as well as means across nationalities, and using qualification tiers to separate content-dependent from content-invariant bias

full_citation: Wilson, K., & Caliskan, A. (2024). Gender, race, and intersectional bias in resume screening via language model retrieval. Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, 7, 1578-1590.
models_or_system: Massive Text Embedding (MTE) retrieval models (cosine similarity), not generative scoring
population_categories: US; race (Black/White) x gender via names
manipulation: Names added to real resumes; retrieval against job descriptions
main_result: White-associated names favoured in 85.1% of cases; Black males disadvantaged in up to 100% of cases. ERRATUM (arXiv v3, 29 Aug 2026): a code bug inverted the gender-only results (reported male preference is female preference and vice versa); race and intersectional results unaffected and replicated by a Salzburg team
limitations: Embedding retrieval rather than instruction-following LLM; published gender results inverted per erratum
relation_to_project: Cite only race/intersectional findings and the erratum; shows name corpus frequency and document length affect outcomes: supports holding length/format constant across clones

full_citation: Yin, L., Alba, D., & Nicoletti, L. (2024, March). OpenAI's GPT is a recruiter's dream tool. Tests show there's racial bias. Bloomberg (data journalism).
population_categories: US; race x gender via names from voter/Census data
manipulation: Ranking of eight near-identical resumes across hundreds of names for four jobs (per README)
main_result: Not verified from the article (paywalled/403); headline claims racial bias in GPT resume ranking
limitations: Journalism; article text not read; byline confirmed via secondary pages only
relation_to_project: Context for public salience of LLM hiring audits; cite only as journalism

full_citation: Veldanda, A. K., Grob, F., Thakur, S., Pearce, H., Tan, B., Karri, R., & Garg, S. (2023). Are Emily and Greg still more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? Investigating algorithmic hiring bias in the era of ChatGPT. arXiv:2310.05135. [Workshop version: 'Investigating Hiring Bias in Large Language Models', NeurIPS 2023 R0-FoMo Workshop.]
venue: arXiv preprint; NeurIPS 2023 R0-FoMo workshop (different title)
population_categories: US; gender, race, maternity status, pregnancy status, political affiliation
manipulation: Protected attributes (e.g., names) on otherwise identical resumes
main_result: LLMs robust across race and gender; differences on pregnancy status and political affiliation
limitations: Preprint/workshop; classification task rather than screening decision
relation_to_project: Null race/gender results in an early audit illustrate task dependence; supports using decision-like outcomes (fit score, interview yes/no, forced choice)

full_citation: Chen, Q., & Xiao, Y. (2026). Beyond the name: Demographic leakage in de-identified resumes and evaluation artifacts in LLM bias audits. arXiv:2609.16501.
population_categories: Five ethnocultural conditions (Anglo, First Nations, Chinese, Indian, Vietnamese) x three cue-salience tiers; an Australian context is inferred from the group set, author affiliations and cited Australian Public Service work, not stated as the study setting
manipulation: Ethnocultural cues in unstructured prose with language fields held identical; counterfactual resumes; pairwise judge with ties forbidden / neutral / encouraged
outcome: Demographic recoverability; pairwise selection; shortlist and 0-100 score
main_result: Target-group recovery 0.757 overall, 1.000 at high salience; forbidding ties gives an apparent selection-rate ratio of 0.39 with strong position and content effects, permitting ties yields >=94% ties for 7 of 9 models; downstream score differences very small
limitations: Preprint under review; setting not stated (Australian context inferred)
relation_to_project: Verdict space drives pairwise results: supports NOT hard-constraining the A/B choice, treating ties/refusals as data, and pre-registering tie handling with a sensitivity analysis

full_citation: Chen, Q., & Xiao, Y. (2026). Competence-Preserving Resume Perturbations Expose Presentation Sensitivity in LLM Screening. arXiv:2609.16517.
models_or_system: Six open instruction-tuned LLM conditions incl. Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.3 (native vs other chat templates)
population_categories: None (no demographic manipulation)
manipulation: Occupation-grounded candidate profiles at controlled competence levels rendered into multiple resume presentations; a deterministic validation gate excludes variants that alter the qualification evidence
outcome: Screening validity; pairwise decision flip rate under presentation changes
main_result: Llama-3.1-8B with its native chat template reaches the highest validity (0.781) yet reverses 29.6% of matched pairwise decisions under competence-preserving presentation changes; Mistral-7B-v0.3 validity 0.644 with a 41.4% flip rate; native chat formatting improves validity but does not remove instability
limitations: Preprint; no demographic factor
relation_to_project: Direct evidence that non-substantive changes often flip LLM screening decisions: motivates an empirical noise floor for 'heterogeneity' (placebo one-line changes, replicate reference clones), identical rendering across clones, logging the chat template, and the positive control as a yardstick

full_citation: Tonneau, M., Sehgal, N. K. R., Malhotra, N., Kazemi, S., Orozco-Olvera, V., Munoz Boudet, A. M., Subramanian, L., Fraiberger, S. P., Guntuku, S. C., & Hofmann, V. (2026). Different Demographic Cues Yield Inconsistent Conclusions About LLM Personalization and Bias. arXiv:2601.18486 (EMNLP 2026).
population_categories: Race and gender (US) via multiple cue types
manipulation: Different cues for the same group in advice-seeking prompts

full_citation: Tamkin, A., Askell, A., Lovitt, L., Durmus, E., Joseph, N., Kravec, S., Nguyen, K., Kaplan, J., & Ganguli, D. (2023). Evaluating and Mitigating Discrimination in Language Model Decisions. arXiv:2312.03689.

full_citation: Arnoult, É., Ruault, M., Valat, E., Villedieu, P., Breda, T., Jacquemet, N., Laouénan, M., Rathelot, R., Safi, M., Sultan Parraud, J., Allegre, A., Bagramova, A., Bouvier, F., Foroni, F., Ftoh Fennane, S., Huet, I., Kozma, B., Medaghri Alaoui, A., & Tekle, E. (2021). Discrimination à l'embauche des personnes d'origine supposée maghrébine : quels enseignements d'une grande étude par testing ? Notes IPP n°76 (also issued as Dares Analyses n°67), November 2021.
venue: Notes IPP n°76 / Dares Analyses n°67 (Dares, Institut des politiques publiques, ISM Corum; grey literature)
population_categories: France (all of metropolitan France); presumed Maghrebi vs presumed French origin x gender; 11 occupation categories; three age bands
manipulation: First name + surname only (Maghrebi- vs French-sounding; first names drawn from the TeO survey and also varied by social class). No nationality on any CV; the authors state that an absent nationality is read as French nationality. 'Maghrebi' is one pooled category
sample_size: 9,600 applications to 2,400 job ads (4 per ad); Dec 2019 to Apr 2021
main_result: Callback 33.3% (French-sounding) vs 22.8% (Maghrebi-sounding): 31.5% lower, ratio 1.5, p<0.01. Gap large in every occupation category except store manager. Low-skilled jobs 33.0% vs 18.1%; managers without supervision 38.1% vs 28.8%; managers with supervision 24.5% vs 20.1%. Oldest age band (48-55, n = 960): 14.0% vs 12.7%, shown without significance stars. Tight occupations: 26% gap vs 34% elsewhere (difference n.s. once controls are added). No origin x gender interaction. 63% of ads treated all four applicants alike
limitations: Grey literature, not peer-reviewed. Read as Note IPP n°76; the Dares Analyses n°67 page is behind a bot wall. Table 3 was garbled in text extraction: re-check the age-band row before citing. One pooled Maghrebi group, names only. Fieldwork overlaps COVID-19
relation_to_project: Largest recent French test and the strongest single source for a 'well documented' claim about North African-origin names in France. The human signal is a name with nationality deliberately absent, the opposite of our explicit Nationality line. Weaker gap in qualified jobs parallels our tier x nationality check

full_citation: Foroni, F., Ruault, M., & Valat, E. (2016). Discrimination à l'embauche selon « l'origine » : que nous apprend le testing auprès de grandes entreprises ? Dares Analyses n°076, December 2016.
venue: Dares Analyses n°076 (French Ministry of Labour; grey literature)
population_categories: France; 40 firms with more than 1,000 employees; 'hexagonal' vs 'Maghrebi' applicants; men and women; employee- and manager-level posts
manipulation: First name + surname on paired, otherwise equivalent applications submitted through firms' career sites; pooled Maghrebi category
sample_size: 1,500 paired tests = 3,000 applications; each firm tested 30 to 40 times; Apr to Jul 2016
main_result: Positive responses 47% ('hexagonal') vs 36% ('Maghrebi'), gap 11 points; only the hexagonal applicant favoured in 20% of tests vs only the Maghrebi applicant in 9%. Gap present for men and women, for employee posts (12 points) and manager posts (9 points). Firms differ: 12 of 40 show a statistically significant gap (15 to 35 points); the report says equal treatment was most often applied by the majority of the 40 firms
limitations: Grey literature. Large firms only, chosen because they post many ads. 30-40 tests per firm gives low power, so 'no significant gap' in 28 firms is weak evidence of no discrimination. Read from a web.archive.org copy (Dares site bot-walled)
relation_to_project: Firm-level heterogeneity in humans, the analogue of model-level heterogeneity in our audit. Average penalty smaller than in arnoult2021discrimination (ratio about 1.3)

full_citation: Cediey, E., & Foroni, F. (2008). Discrimination in access to employment on grounds of foreign origin in France: A national survey of discrimination based on the testing methodology of the International Labour Office. International Migration Papers 85E. Geneva: International Labour Office.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (ILO situation testing: matched pairs by telephone, CV and in person)
population_categories: France; six urban areas (Lille, Lyon, Marseille, Nantes, Paris, Strasbourg); young French men and women of ostensible North African or sub-Saharan origin vs 'metropolitan French origin'; low- and medium/low-skilled jobs
manipulation: First name + family name (e.g. Kader or Farida Larbi, Farid or Latifa Boukhrit); all testers French nationals; each site tested one origin and one gender
sample_size: 2,440 tests, of which 1,100 valid and usable; end 2005 to mid 2006
outcome: Which applicant the employer favours across the whole recruitment process; net discrimination rate
main_result: Employers favoured the majority applicant in 70% of usable tests and the minority applicant in 19% (net 51%); equal treatment throughout in 11%. North African origin, men: net rate 45.9% (Lyon) and 48.8% (Lille). North African origin, women: 27.4% (Strasbourg), the lowest rate in the survey. Sub-Saharan origin: 53.9% (men, Nantes), 45.4% and 56.0% (women, Marseille and Paris)
limitations: Origin, gender and site are confounded (one combination per site), so North African vs sub-Saharan and men vs women comparisons are not clean; the authors say so. In-person stages are not blind. Grey literature. Summary, design and results parts read, not the whole 122 pages
relation_to_project: Early large French benchmark. North African origin is penalised heavily but not more than sub-Saharan origin; lowest rate recorded was for North African-origin women

full_citation: Duguet, E., Leandri, N., L'Horty, Y., & Petit, P. (2010). Are young French jobseekers of ethnic immigrant origin discriminated against? A controlled experiment in the Paris area. Annals of Economics and Statistics, 99/100, 187-215.
population_categories: France, Paris region; young men aged 20-22; accountant posts; Moroccan vs French origin; privileged vs underprivileged town of residence
manipulation: Three separate cues: Moroccan nationality stated explicitly on the CV (French applicants state no nationality), Moroccan- vs French-sounding surname, Moroccan- vs French-sounding first name. One origin country (Morocco)
sample_size: 1,097 CVs to 140 vacancies; 16 profiles; end of 2006
main_result: Success rates: French names, nationality not stated 7.27% (20/275); Moroccan surname + French first name 2.90% (8/276); Moroccan surname and first name, French nationality 1.84% (5/272); Moroccan names + stated Moroccan nationality 0.36% (1/274). Index 100 / 40 / 25 / 5. Pure nationality effect (same Moroccan names, nationality stated or not): 1.45 points, just significant at 10%. Surname and first-name effects n.s. separately, significant combined. No major gap by place of residence
limitations: Very low base rate (34 successes in 1,097 CVs), so estimates are imprecise. Men only, one occupation, one origin. Numbers read in the working-paper version (TEPP WP 2010-1, revised July 2009), not the journal PDF
relation_to_project: Closest human precedent for our manipulation: an explicit nationality line, separated from the name cue. The name carried most of the penalty; the nationality line added little on top of a Moroccan name. Our CVs have no name, so the nationality line carries the whole signal and sizes are not comparable
novelty_threat_reason: Human; states one Arab nationality (Moroccan) explicitly; no within-Arab comparison

full_citation: Edo, A., Jacquemet, N., & Yannelis, C. (2019). Language skills and homophilous hiring discrimination: Evidence from gender and racially differentiated applications. Review of Economics of the Household, 17(1), 349-376.
venue: Review of Economics of the Household
population_categories: France (Paris area); accounting-sector jobs; French-, North African- and unidentifiable 'foreign'-sounding names x gender
manipulation: Names only, pre-tested in a survey (North African names identified by 98%; 'foreign' names seen as foreign by 94-96% with no origin identified). A French-language-skill signal was added to all CVs for half of the ads
main_result: Callback: French 17.3%, North African 9.9%, unidentifiable foreign 10.1%; North African vs foreign difference n.s. Men 14.9 / 7.1 / 8.1%; women 19.5 / 12.7 / 12.1%. Ratios about 2 for men and 1.6 for women. The language signal narrows the gap for women (North African women 10.7% to 14.7%) and much less for men

full_citation: Pierné, G. (2013). Hiring discrimination based on national origin and religious closeness: Results from a field experiment in the Paris area. IZA Journal of Labor Economics, 2, 4.
population_categories: France, Paris and suburbs; real-estate jobs; male applicants; North African vs French origin x secular / Catholic / Muslim closeness
manipulation: Origin via first + last name; religion via the organisation named under volunteering (secular, Catholic or Muslim). Pooled 'North African'
sample_size: 1,800 résumés to 300 vacancies; mid-April to mid-September 2011
main_result: Callback: French secular 32.00%, French Catholic 31.67%, French Muslim 20.33%; North African secular 16.67%, North African Catholic 17.67%, North African Muslim 11.33%. Origin gap about 15 points whatever the religion signal (9 points among Muslim-signalling applicants). Muslim closeness costs French applicants 11.33 points and North African applicants 6.33 points; Catholic closeness has no effect
limitations: One sector, men only, Paris area
relation_to_project: Origin and religion penalties are separable and both present: a North African name is penalised even with a Catholic signal. Supports treating religion as one part of the total effect of an Arab nationality signal, not all of it

full_citation: Valfort, M.-A. (2020). Anti-Muslim discrimination in France: Evidence from a field experiment. World Development, 135, 105022.
population_categories: France; fictitious applicants who all originate from Lebanon; Muslim vs Christian; religious vs not; ordinary vs outstanding; men and women
manipulation: Inherited religion and adult religiosity (Scouting membership) varied while origin country is held constant (Lebanon); details in valfort2015discriminations
sample_size: not stated in abstract (6,231 job ads according to the 2015 report on the same experiment)
main_result: No discrimination against Muslims who are not religious. Religious Muslims lose ground unless outstanding; religiosity is a premium for Christians; religious Muslims must send twice as many applications as religious Christians. Gap concentrated among ordinary religious men (4.2% vs 10.9%)
limitations: Abstract only (HAL record; publisher 403, HAL PDF bot-walled). Compares Muslim vs Christian within Lebanese origin; there is no native-French comparator, so it does not measure an origin penalty The working-paper version (IZA DP 11417, 2018), read in full in part L5, reports 4.7% vs 17.9% for religious men; cite the journal figures.
relation_to_project: Key null: among Lebanese-origin applicants a Muslim signal without religiosity carried no penalty. Religiosity, not Arab origin as such, drives this result. Our nationality line carries no religiosity cue
novelty_threat_reason: Human; one Arab origin (Lebanon) held constant

full_citation: Valfort, M.-A. (2015). Discriminations religieuses à l'embauche : une réalité. Paris: Institut Montaigne.
population_categories: France; French citizens of Lebanese origin born in Beirut in 1988, arrived 2003, naturalised 2008; Catholic, Jewish, Muslim; practising vs secular; ordinary vs exceptional; accounting jobs
manipulation: Same surname (Haddad) and Arabic mother tongue for all. Religion via first name (Michel/Nathalie, Dov/Esther, Mohammed/Samira), confessional school in Beirut and scouting association. Birth in Lebanon and naturalisation are stated in the CV and cover letter
main_result: Practising applicants: Catholic 20.8%, Jewish 15.8%, Muslim 10.4%. Men: Catholic 17.9% vs Muslim 4.7% (nearly 4 times); women: Catholics about 40% above Muslims. Ordinary Muslim men who present as secular reach response rates equivalent to ordinary practising Catholic men
limitations: Think-tank report on the same experiment as valfort2020anti. One origin country, one sector, no native-French comparator. Summary, design and main results sections read, not all 142 pages
relation_to_project: Human precedent for stating origin country and citizenship history explicitly on the CV while varying another cue. Strong gender asymmetry: men are penalised far more
novelty_threat_reason: Human; one Arab origin (Lebanon) held constant

full_citation: Challe, L., L'Horty, Y., Petit, P., & Wolff, F.-C. (2024). Cyclical behavior of hiring discrimination: Evidence from repeated experiments in France. The Annals of Regional Science, 72(3), 711-733.
population_categories: France; male applicants for administrative-manager posts, private and public sector; French origin vs North African descent (French citizens); neutral vs deprived neighbourhood
manipulation: First name + surname (e.g. Mehdi, Karim, Mounir; Benchargui, Mokraoui, Mehdaoui); pooled North African
sample_size: 4,749 applications to 1,583 openings in five waves (554, 384, 248, 194, 203 openings); Oct 2015 to Oct 2020
main_result: The North African candidate was 'almost systematically' below the reference 'although the differences were not always significant'. Wave 1 (2015-16): significant only in the public sector (reference 31.1%, North African 8.7 points lower). Waves 2-3: 'very few significant differences' (exception: private sector 2019, 7 points). Wave 4 (lockdown, spring 2020): no ethnic discrimination detected in either sector. Wave 5 (autumn 2020): private-sector penalty 17.2 points, significant at 1%; no significant difference in the public sector
limitations: One occupation, men only. Waves 3-5 are small (about 200-250 openings; the authors compute power 0.415 at n = 200 for a 5-point gap), so the nulls are weak evidence of absence
relation_to_project: Best documented set of nulls: same design and occupation, and the gap comes and goes with the labour market. A blanket 'well documented' claim should allow for context dependence

full_citation: Ene Jones, E. (2013). Discrimination à l'embauche des jeunes en Île-de-France : un diplôme plus élevé compense-t-il une origine maghrébine ? Économie et Statistique, 464(1), 173-188.
population_categories: France, Île-de-France; young men; maintenance-technician posts; Maghrebi vs French origin x diploma level
manipulation: Origin signalled by first name + surname (per the report version); one of two Maghrebi-origin applicants holds a higher diploma (BTS vs Bac)
sample_size: 441 applications to 147 job ads; late July to late August 2010
main_result: Discriminatory practices against Maghrebi-origin applicants, only weakly offset by a higher diploma: the better-qualified Maghrebi-origin applicant does better than the other one but still worse than the French-origin applicant
limitations: Abstract only; rates not read. Small, one occupation, men only. Crossref lists the author as 'Ene Jones, Emilia'; the TEPP report version (2012-5) gives 'Emilia Ene'
relation_to_project: Extra qualification did not close the gap, in contrast to kaas2012ethnic where reference letters did. Relevant to our qualification-tier check

full_citation: Behaghel, L., Crépon, B., & Le Barbanchon, T. (2015). Unintended effects of anonymous résumés. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 7(3), 1-27.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (randomised policy experiment with real jobseekers; not a correspondence audit)
population_categories: France; real candidates sent by the public employment service; 'minority' = residents of deprived neighbourhoods, immigrants or children of immigrants (not MENA-specific; the data also flag African- or Muslim-sounding names)
manipulation: Résumés anonymised (name, address, gender, nationality, photo, age removed) vs standard, randomised among firms that agreed to take part
sample_size: About 600 participating firms; 62% of invited firms agreed; Nov 2009 to Sep 2010
outcome: Interview and hiring rates of minority vs majority candidates
main_result: Participating firms became less likely to interview and hire minority candidates when résumés were anonymous. The authors explain this by self-selection of firms into the programme and by anonymisation removing the attenuation of negative signals for minority candidates
limitations: Not a measure of discrimination levels. Self-selected firms; composite minority category. Abstract, introduction and data section read (IZA DP 8517), results tables not read
relation_to_project: Reversal in a selected sample: with names visible, minority candidates did better than under anonymity. Warning for our not-stated control: removing the cue is not a neutral baseline

full_citation: Baert, S., Albanese, A., du Gardein, S., Ovaere, J., & Stappers, J. (2017). Does work experience mitigate discrimination? Economics Letters, 155, 35-38.
population_categories: Belgium (Flanders, Ghent area); Flemish vs Turkish, Moroccan, Slovakian and Ghanaian names; recent graduates, 10 or 20 years of experience
manipulation: Names only (frequent, non-stereotypical names supplied by the Ghent city administration); all pairs hold Belgian nationality; the four origins alternate
main_result: Natives invited in 11.2% of applications, immigrant-named candidates in 7.8% (ratio 0.698, about 30% fewer, p<0.01). Recent graduates 50.0% fewer and those with 10 years' experience 35.7% fewer (both p<0.05); at 20 years' experience the ratio is slightly above 1 and n.s. By origin, relative to Slovakian names: Turkish -0.073 (p<0.05), Ghanaian -0.062 (p<0.10), Moroccan -0.042 (SE 0.033, n.s.)
limitations: Small sample; per-origin n not read; Ghent area only. Read in the UGent postprint
relation_to_project: Null in a subgroup: no detectable penalty for very experienced applicants. Moroccan-named applicants were not distinguishable from Slovakian-named ones. Predicts weaker effects in our strong-tier CVs

full_citation: Lippens, L., Dalle, A., D'hondt, F., Verhaeghe, P.-P., & Baert, S. (2023). Understanding ethnic hiring discrimination: A contextual analysis of experimental evidence. Labour Economics, 85, 102453.
population_categories: Belgium (Flanders: Antwerp and Ghent); Flemish vs Maghrebian (Moroccan), Turkish, Eastern European (Slovakian) and sub-Saharan African names; gender and experience varied between pairs
manipulation: Names only; all candidates Belgian nationals
sample_size: 890 vacancies (paired applications): Maghrebian 283, Turkish 282, Eastern European 163, sub-Saharan African 162; fieldwork during COVID-19
outcome: Any positive response; invitation to interview
main_result: Any positive response: minorities overall 15.82% fewer (p<0.001). Maghrebian 21.49% fewer (ratio 78.51%, p = 0.006); Turkish 14.57% fewer (p = 0.039); Eastern European 26.51% fewer (p = 0.002), the largest gap; sub-Saharan African ratio exactly 1. Interview invitations only: only the Turkish effect is significant at 5%. Less discrimination in not-for-profit and in large organisations. The authors note that Belgians distinguish Belgian from non-Belgian names but not specific origins
limitations: COVID-period labour market; names only; two small groups. Table 2 was garbled in text extraction, so the figures are taken from the running text
relation_to_project: Maghrebian penalty present but not the largest, and not significant on the strict interview outcome. The authors' own warning that names do not convey a specific origin supports our explicit nationality field

full_citation: Martiniello, B., & Verhaeghe, P.-P. (2022). Signaling ethnic-national origin through names? The perception of names from an intersectional perspective. PLoS ONE, 17(8), e0270990.
population_categories: Belgium (Flanders); 180 names of Belgian, Moroccan, Turkish, Polish and Congolese origin, homogeneous and mixed
manipulation: Names rated for ethnic-national origin, gender, religiosity, social class and education
outcome: Congruence between perceived and intended origin
main_result: HUMAN: 'respondents distinguish Belgian from non-Belgian names rather than perceiving a specific ethnic-national origin'; non-Belgian names are recognised as non-Belgian at about 95.5% (mixed) to 98.5% (homogeneous), but only 48.2% of homogeneous Moroccan names are identified as non-European and 34% are assigned to Morocco (Turkish names: 34.5% to Turkey); homogeneous Moroccan and Turkish names are mostly perceived as religious (45.8% and 40.6%)
limitations: HUMAN; Flanders only; one Arab origin (Moroccan), so confusion among Arab nationalities is not measured directly; what Moroccan names were mistaken for was not extracted; Table 1 is row-shifted in the text extraction, so only figures confirmed in the running text are quoted
relation_to_project: Direct support for the methodological point in our introduction: names signal 'foreign' and 'Muslim', not a specific country, so name-based audits cannot separate Arab national origins. Justifies the explicit Nationality line

full_citation: Thijssen, L., Coenders, M., & Lancee, B. (2021). Ethnic discrimination in the Dutch labor market: Differences between ethnic minority groups and the role of personal information about job applicants - Evidence from a field experiment. Journal of International Migration and Integration, 22(3), 1125-1150.
venue: Journal of International Migration and Integration
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (GEMM field experiment, Dutch arm)
population_categories: Netherlands; native Dutch vs 35 minority groups, grouped into 7 regions of origin incl. Middle East and North Africa; Moroccan, Turkish, Polish and Bulgarian oversampled; 10 occupations; men and women
manipulation: First + last name, origin-country language listed as mother tongue, and a cover-letter sentence that the applicant or the parents were born abroad but all schooling was in the Netherlands
outcome: Positive response (invitation or request for information)
main_result: Predicted positive response 46% for native Dutch vs 35% for migrant origin (about 11 points). By region: MENA 31% (-14.3 points), South and Central African 32%, Latin American 33%; Western European/American 39%. By group: Moroccan 31%, Turkish 32%, Antillean 27%, Surinamese 36%, Bulgarian 35%, Polish 40% (no significant evidence of discrimination). No ethnicity x gender interaction; no clear variation by occupation or region; adding personal information does not reduce the gap
limitations: MENA analysed as one pooled region; only Moroccan and Turkish estimated separately. The list of origin groups (Supplement Table S2) was not read
relation_to_project: Shows the practice we question: many origins collected, then pooled into one MENA region for analysis. MENA is not uniquely worst here; sub-Saharan African and Latin American origins are similar
novelty_threat_reason: Human multi-origin audit with a pooled MENA region (same GEMM family as koopmans2019taste); no within-Arab estimates reported

full_citation: Andriessen, I., Nievers, E., Dagevos, J., & Faulk, L. (2012). Ethnic discrimination in the Dutch labor market: Its relationship with job characteristics and multiple group membership. Work and Occupations, 39(3), 237-269.
population_categories: Netherlands; Dutch-sounding names vs names signalling immigrant descent (groups not named in the abstract; thijssen2021ethnic describes them as Moroccan, Turkish, Surinamese and Antillean)
manipulation: Names
sample_size: 2,080 applications to 1,340 vacancies (as stated in the abstract)
main_result: Abstract: 'discrimination continues to be a problem in selection procedures'; interactions with job characteristics and multiple group membership are discussed; no effect sizes in the abstract. Secondary description in thijssen2021ethnic: similar levels of discrimination against Moroccan, Turkish, Surinamese and Antillean applicants
limitations: Abstract only; group-level results known only from a secondary source
relation_to_project: Dutch benchmark in which the Moroccan penalty is reported as similar to that of non-MENA minority groups
novelty_threat_reason: Human; one Arab origin (Moroccan) among four groups

full_citation: Ramos, M., Thijssen, L., & Coenders, M. (2021). Labour market discrimination against Moroccan minorities in the Netherlands and Spain: A cross-national and cross-regional comparison. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 47(6), 1261-1284.
venue: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
population_categories: Netherlands and Spain; applicants of Moroccan origin vs native majority
manipulation: Cross-nationally standardised fictitious applications; signal not stated in the abstract
main_result: Moroccan-origin applicants are 6 percentage points less likely to get a positive response in Spain; the predicted gap in the Netherlands is 14 points. Regional differences unrelated to regional unemployment; in the Netherlands a larger regional share of Moroccans goes with more discrimination
limitations: Abstract only (tandfonline 403)
relation_to_project: Same origin, very different penalty depending on destination country: context dependence. One Arab origin only

full_citation: Derous, E., Ryan, A. M., & Nguyen, H.-H. D. (2012). Multiple categorization in resume screening: Examining effects on hiring discrimination against Arab applicants in field and lab settings. Journal of Organizational Behavior, 33(4), 544-570.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers and raters (two correspondence tests, one lab study, one field experiment with recruiters)
population_categories: Netherlands; Arab vs Dutch applicants x sex x socio-economic status x job type
manipulation: not stated in abstract ('ethnic group membership (Arabic)'); pooled Arab category
outcome: Rejection (correspondence tests); hiring evaluations (lab and recruiter studies)
main_result: Low-status jobs: odds of rejection four times higher for Arab than for Dutch applicants; sex, socio-economic status and client contact did not moderate (Study 1). Raters' motivation to control prejudice moderated the effect (Study 2). Double jeopardy against Arab women for high-status jobs once recruiter prejudice was controlled (Study 3)
limitations: Abstract only; sample sizes and the origin cue not read
relation_to_project: Pooled-Arab Dutch evidence; gender effect depends on job status and on the study

full_citation: Derous, E., Ryan, A. M., & Serlie, A. W. (2015). Double jeopardy upon resumé screening: When Achmed is less employable than Aïsha. Personnel Psychology, 68(3), 659-696.
models_or_system: HUMAN recruiters (two field experiments in which professional recruiters rate résumés; not a correspondence audit of real vacancies)
population_categories: Arab vs majority applicants x sex; low- and high-demand jobs; client contact (country not stated in abstract)
manipulation: Applicant ethnicity and sex on résumés (cue not stated in abstract); pooled Arab category
main_result: In both low- and high-demand jobs Arab women were rated more favourably than Arab men, particularly where client contact matters. Recruiters high in explicit ethnic prejudice discriminated only when the applicant's qualifications fit the job less (attributional ambiguity). Implicit attitudes played no strong role
limitations: Abstract only; ratings, not real callbacks
relation_to_project: Reverses the 'double jeopardy' expectation: Arab men, not women, fare worst. Penalty appears mainly for weaker-fit CVs, so expect larger effects in our weaker tiers. Our CVs carry no gender signal

full_citation: Busetta, G., Campolo, M. G., & Panarello, D. (2018). Immigrants and Italian labor market: Statistical or taste-based discrimination? Genus, 74, 4.
population_categories: Italy (applicants resident in Rome, online job postings); Italian vs first- and second-generation Moroccan, Romanian, Albanian, Chinese and German applicants; men and women
manipulation: Name, surname, city of birth, mother tongue and place of schooling; second-generation applicants are born in Rome but do not hold Italian nationality; no photo. Split by nationality (one Arab: Morocco)
sample_size: 22,000 CVs to 1,000 job postings (Jul 2013 to Oct 2014); analysis sample 5,038 CVs from the 229 firms that replied to at least one
main_result: Callback in the restricted sample: Italian 52%, second generation 32%, first generation 24% (full sample 12% / 7% / 5%). Moroccan and Chinese applicants are the most discriminated, Germans the least. Second-generation Moroccan vs Italian: net discrimination 47.83% in graduate jobs (relative callback 2.03), 37.39% in high-school jobs (1.73), 44.92% in front-office jobs (2.00). Women get fewer callbacks than men in every group; the gender gap among Italians exceeds the Italian-immigrant gap
limitations: Restricting to firms that replied inflates rates; all applicants live in Rome
relation_to_project: Rare human design in which nationality is the treatment across five national origins. Moroccan sits at the bottom with Chinese while German (rich, EU) is barely penalised: a status gradient like our H1d, already present in humans
novelty_threat_reason: Human; five nationalities but only one Arab (Moroccan)

full_citation: Bursell, M. (2014). The multiple burdens of foreign-named men - Evidence from a field experiment on gendered ethnic hiring discrimination in Sweden. European Sociological Review, 30(3), 399-409.
population_categories: Sweden; Arabic and North African names vs Swedish names x gender; male- and female-dominated occupations
manipulation: Names; pooled 'Arabic and North African'
main_result: 'Extensive ethnic discrimination' against applicants with Arabic and North African names; no discrimination against women. Male-dominated occupations: gender overcompensation favouring female-named applicants. Female-dominated occupations: 'both ethnic and gender overcompensation, favouring foreign-named men in particular'
limitations: Abstract only; rates and n not read
relation_to_project: Reversal in a sub-context: in female-dominated occupations foreign-named men were favoured. The penalty is not uniform across occupations

full_citation: Vernby, K., & Dancygier, R. (2019). Can immigrants counteract employer discrimination? A factorial field experiment reveals the immutability of ethnic hierarchies. PLOS ONE, 14(7), e0218044.
population_categories: Sweden, seven largest metropolitan areas; restaurant and café jobs; applicants born in Sweden, Poland, Iraq or Somalia who arrived as children; gender, citizenship, work experience and religious activity also varied
manipulation: Country of birth plus names common in that country; Swedish citizenship (yes/no) and a religious-activity signal randomised. Split by origin country
outcome: Callback (job offer, interview invitation or request for contact)
main_result: Callback: Sweden-born 21%, Poland-born 17%, Iraq-born 10%, Somalia-born 5%. Poland vs Iraq/Somalia and Iraq vs Somalia differences significant (p<0.01). Women get more callbacks (Somali men 2.5% vs Somali women 7.5%). Citizenship, experience and religious-activity signals have small, imprecise effects; employers do not prefer immigrant citizens over non-citizens
limitations: One low-skill sector; cover letters built to raise callbacks (e.g. football-club membership); arrived-as-children profile
relation_to_project: Closest human analogue to an explicit national-origin field: the origin country is given, and two Arab League members (Iraq, Somalia) differ significantly from each other. Citizenship made no difference here, whereas quillian2026racialized finds that it matters: relevant to our worry that a nationality line also signals citizenship
novelty_threat_reason: Human; varies two Arab League origins (Iraq, Somalia) by stated country of birth and finds them different; not an LLM study and not framed as within-Arab

full_citation: Carlsson, M. (2010). Experimental evidence of discrimination in the hiring of first- and second-generation immigrants. LABOUR, 24(3), 263-278.
population_categories: Sweden; first- and second-generation immigrants from the Middle East vs natives
manipulation: not stated in abstract; pooled 'Middle East'
main_result: First- and second-generation immigrants from the Middle East have 'essentially the same probability' of an interview invitation, and it is significantly lower than for natives
limitations: Abstract only
relation_to_project: Being locally born did not help: the penalty attaches to the origin signal, not to foreign human capital

full_citation: Dahl, M., & Krog, N. (2018). Experimental evidence of discrimination in the labour market: Intersections between ethnicity, gender, and socio-economic status. European Sociological Review, 34(4), 402-417.
population_categories: Denmark; Danish vs Middle Eastern-sounding names x gender; several occupations
manipulation: Names only, randomly assigned; names also checked for socio-economic connotation; pooled 'Middle Eastern'
main_result: Ethnic discrimination is 'strongly moderated by gender': minority men face a much larger degree of discrimination than minority women across occupation types. Callback differences are attributed to ethnic traits, not to the socio-economic status of the names
limitations: Abstract only; rates and n not read
relation_to_project: Gender asymmetry again: the pooled Middle Eastern penalty is largely a penalty on men. Our CVs carry no gender signal, so models may fill in a default

full_citation: Widner, D., & Chicoine, S. (2011). It's all in the name: Employment discrimination against Arab Americans. Sociological Forum, 26(4), 806-823.
population_categories: United States; white-sounding vs Arab-sounding male names
manipulation: Name randomly assigned to two similar résumés; pooled 'Arab'
sample_size: Résumés sent to 265 jobs over 15 months
main_result: An Arab male applicant needed to send two résumés for every one sent by a white male applicant to receive a callback
limitations: Abstract only. Small; men only; location and occupations not stated in the abstract
relation_to_project: The one US correspondence study found that uses Arab names. US evidence for Arab applicants rests on this single small study

full_citation: Wallace, M., Wright, B. R. E., & Hyde, A. (2014). Religious affiliation and hiring discrimination in the American South. Social Currents, 1(2), 189-207.
population_categories: United States (South); seven religious groups incl. Muslim, plus a control
manipulation: Religious affiliation indicated on the résumé (how is not stated in the abstract); no Arab or national-origin cue
main_result: Applicants expressing any religious identity were 26% less likely to get a response. Muslims, pagans and atheists faced the highest discrimination; Catholics and a fictitious group moderate; evangelical Christians little; Jews none discernible (possibly preferential treatment)
limitations: Abstract only. Religion, not origin
relation_to_project: US evidence concerns Muslim religion rather than Arab origin; the Muslim penalty is shared with atheists and pagans, so it is partly a penalty on religious non-conformity

full_citation: Acquisti, A., & Fong, C. (2020). An experiment in hiring discrimination via online social networks. Management Science, 66(3), 1005-1024.
population_categories: United States; Muslim vs Christian candidate (and gay vs straight)
manipulation: Trait disclosed only on the candidate's social-network profile, not on the résumé
main_result: Nationally, no significant difference in callback rates for the Muslim vs the Christian candidate. Employers in Republican areas show significant bias against the Muslim candidate, significantly larger than in Democratic areas
limitations: Abstract only. The cue is only seen if the employer searches online
relation_to_project: National-level null with a political-context interaction. Religion, not Arab origin

full_citation: Eid, P. (2012). Les inégalités « ethnoraciales » dans l'accès à l'emploi à Montréal : le poids de la discrimination. Recherches sociographiques, 53(2), 415-450.
population_categories: Canada, Montréal; 'Franco-Québécois' names vs Arab, Latin American or African names; skilled and low-skilled jobs
manipulation: Names on paired CVs
main_result: The majority candidate is at least 60% more likely to be invited than the racialised-minority candidates; a little more than one time in three the minority candidate is ignored on a discriminatory basis
limitations: Abstract only; the Arab-specific rate is not stated in the abstract (érudit PDF not retrieved)
relation_to_project: Canadian evidence, French-language. Arab names are one of three minority name groups

full_citation: Beauregard, J.-P., Arteau, G., & Drolet-Brassard, R. (2019). Testing à l'embauche des Québécoises et Québécois d'origine maghrébine à Québec. Recherches sociographiques, 60(1), 35-61.
population_categories: Canada, Québec City metropolitan area; Maghrebi-origin vs majority Québécois applicants, women and men; highly qualified administrative jobs
manipulation: not stated in abstract (title and design indicate names); pooled Maghrebi
sample_size: 404 CVs to 202 job ads; March to July 2017
main_result: Net discrimination rate of 49% against Maghrebi-origin applicants: their application was ignored nearly one time in two on a potentially discriminatory basis. The first 'intersectional test' did not show gender to be a significant factor
limitations: Abstract only. Small
relation_to_project: Canadian evidence for a Maghrebi group specifically; no gender difference

full_citation: Booth, A. L., Leigh, A., & Varganova, E. (2012). Does ethnic discrimination vary across minority groups? Evidence from a field experiment. Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics, 74(4), 547-573.
venue: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics
population_categories: Australia (Brisbane, Melbourne, Sydney); Anglo-Saxon vs Indigenous, Chinese, Italian and Middle Eastern names; men and women; entry-level jobs
manipulation: Names only (taken from behindthename.com); CV states high school in Australia; 'Middle Eastern' is one pooled category
sample_size: Over 4,000 applications; about 840 per group (Middle Eastern n = 845); 2007
main_result: Callback: Anglo-Saxon 35%, Italian 32%, Indigenous 26%, Middle Eastern 22%, Chinese 21%. To get as many interviews, a Middle Eastern applicant must send 64% more applications (Chinese 68%, Indigenous 35%, Italian 12%). Middle Eastern men 19% vs Anglo men 33% (ratio 1.76); women 25% vs 38% (ratio 1.52); the gender difference in discrimination is not significant (p = 0.15)
limitations: Numbers read in the working-paper version (IZA DP 4947, May 2010), not the journal PDF. Names only; entry-level jobs
relation_to_project: Evidence outside Europe. The Middle Eastern penalty is large but equal to the Chinese one, so MENA is not uniquely targeted. Their census definition of 'Middle Eastern' puts Arab states together with Iran, Israel and Turkey: the pooling we question

full_citation: Adamovic, M., & Leibbrandt, A. (2023). Is there a glass ceiling for ethnic minorities to enter leadership positions? Evidence from a field experiment with over 12,000 job applications. The Leadership Quarterly, 34(2), 101655.
population_categories: Australia (Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane); English vs Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Arabic, Chinese, Greek and Indian names; leadership and non-leadership jobs
manipulation: Names only, pre-tested (Arabic names correctly identified by 88% in one check and over 93% in another); pooled 'Arabic'
main_result: Leadership jobs: English names 26.8% vs Arabic 9.7% (lowest of the six groups; Chinese 10.3%, Indian 10.8%, Aboriginal 11.8%, Greek 14.3%). Non-leadership jobs: English 21.2% vs Arabic 10.0% (Indian 9.8%, Chinese 12.3%, Aboriginal 12.4%, Greek 13.7%)
limitations: Names only; the regression tables were not read in detail
relation_to_project: Recent large study with a pooled Arabic-name group; Arabic names are at or near the bottom, but the Indian and Chinese penalties are of the same size

full_citation: Quillian, L., & Lee, J. J. (2023). Trends in racial and ethnic discrimination in hiring in six Western countries. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 120(6), e2212875120.
population_categories: Canada, France, Germany, Great Britain, Netherlands, United States; African/Black, Asian, Latin American/Hispanic, and Middle Eastern/North African (MENA, incl. Turkish) groups
manipulation: not applicable (meta-regression on year)
sample_size: 90 studies, 140 effects, 174,079 applications; MENA: 41 effects from 37 studies; 1969 to 2019
main_result: Discrimination against MENA-origin groups rose after 2000: decade indicators for 2001-2010 and after 2010 are significantly above the 1990s (discrimination ratio up about 40% in the baseline model). The linear trend for MENA is positive but not significantly different from zero; no MENA studies exist before 1990. Other groups are flat. France declined from very high to high; the Netherlands increased. The same pattern holds for Muslim-majority origins
limitations: MENA is a pooled category that includes Turkish. SI tables not read
relation_to_project: Post-2020 multi-country synthesis with a pooled MENA estimate. The authors justify broad categories because 'ethnic distinctions within these categories are often incorrectly perceived by outsiders': the counter-argument to our disaggregation, which does not apply once nationality is written on the CV

full_citation: Polavieja, J. G., Lancee, B., Ramos, M., Veit, S., & Yemane, R. (2023). In your face: A comparative field experiment on racial discrimination in Europe. Socio-Economic Review, 21(3), 1551-1578.
population_categories: Germany, Netherlands, Spain; young-adult country nationals born to parents from over 40 countries of ancestry; four phenotypic groups x four regions of ancestry
manipulation: Ancestry 'signaled foremost by name'; racial appearance by photograph
main_result: Phenotype has a significant, independent effect on employers' responses in Germany and the Netherlands; in Spain discrimination appears only for particular combinations of phenotype and ancestry
limitations: Verified at abstract level only. The publisher page was reachable only through an automated page reader, which returned, unchecked: MENA ancestry = Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Morocco, Turkey; white MENA-ancestry applicants have 25% (Germany) to 35% (Netherlands) lower odds of a callback. Re-read before citing
relation_to_project: GEMM data again: several Arab ancestries collected, analysed as one MENA region. Spain shows a much weaker pattern than Germany or the Netherlands
novelty_threat_reason: Human; GEMM data with several Arab ancestries pooled into one MENA region (per an unchecked extract)

full_citation: Fernández-Reino, M., Di Stasio, V., & Veit, S. (2023). Discrimination unveiled: A field experiment on the barriers faced by Muslim women in Germany, the Netherlands, and Spain. European Sociological Review, 39(3), 479-497.
population_categories: Germany, Netherlands, Spain; veiled and unveiled Muslim women
manipulation: Muslim signal via volunteering in a Muslim community centre, or via the headscarf
main_result: Veiled Muslim women are discriminated against in Germany and the Netherlands, but only when applying for jobs with a high level of customer contact. In Spain discrimination against veiled Muslim women is much smaller
limitations: Abstract only; the result for unveiled Muslim women vs majority women and the origin countries are not stated in the abstract
relation_to_project: The penalty depends on a visible religious practice and on job type, not only on origin. We use no photo and no religion cue

full_citation: Ariel, B., Tobby-Alimi, I., Cohen, I., Ben Ezra, M., Cohen, Y., & Sosinski, G. (2015). Ethnic and racial employment discrimination in low-wage and high-wage markets: Randomized controlled trials using correspondence tests in Israel. The Law & Ethics of Human Rights, 9(1), 113-139.
venue: The Law & Ethics of Human Rights
population_categories: Israel; Israeli-Arab vs Jewish lawyers applying to the largest law firms (n = 178); Mizrahi vs Ashkenazi Jews applying to security firms (n = 369)
manipulation: Correspondence tests; the abstract describes the cue only generically (e.g. the applicant's name)
sample_size: n = 178 (law firms) and n = 369 (security firms); seven independent tests
outcome: Acknowledgement of application; invitation to interview
main_result: Significant overall discrimination against Arab-Israelis and Mizrahi Jews, whose applications are less likely to be acknowledged and to lead to an interview. In low-wage jobs the effect depends on location, and in some regions there is no preference toward either group
limitations: Abstract only. Arabs here are a native minority, not migrants
relation_to_project: The only field experiment found that is set inside the Middle East. No study was found in which Arab applicants of different nationalities apply inside an Arab country, so the setting of our stimuli has no human benchmark in this search

full_citation: Albaroudi, E., Mansouri, T., Hatamleh, M., & Alameer, A. (2026). Addressing intersectional bias in AI recruitment using HITHIRE model: a fair, ethical, green AI and transparent hiring solution for Saudi Arabia's diverse workforce in line with vision 2030. AI and Ethics, 6(1), 57. (Published online 11 Dec 2025.)
models_or_system: Baseline CV-job matchers: Llama 3.1 (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), BERT, 'regular NLP'; HITHIRE = modified Llama 3.1 pipeline
population_categories: Saudi labour-market framing; gender; nationality coded Arab vs non-Arab. 18 Arab nationalities are named (Emirati, Saudi, Qatari, Kuwaiti, Omani, Bahraini, Jordanian, Lebanese, Egyptian, Syrian, Iraqi, Palestinian, Sudanese, Yemeni, Moroccan, Algerian, Tunisian, Libyan) but pooled into one 'Arab' group in every model-level metric
manipulation: None (observational). Real CVs carrying a nationality field, matched to job descriptions (HR, IT, finance); ground truth = accept/reject labels from one HR manager; no counterfactual clones, qualifications not held fixed
outcome: Predicted accept/reject; group-fairness metrics (SPD, DI, AOD, EOD, Theil) for Arab vs non-Arab and gender x nationality
main_result: Llama 3.1 baseline, nationality: SPD 0.4367, DI 1.1473, AOD and EOD 0.0 (Table 11); HITHIRE: SPD 0.1464, DI 1.2387. Direction not interpretable: the text reads the same DI of 1.1473 once as Arabs favoured by 14.73% and once as non-Arabs favoured by 14.73%. Baseline subgroups (SPD / DI): female Arab -0.0214 / 0.9476, male Arab -0.0356 / 0.9129.
